hypotheses.d: Documented pressure on Assembly electors, 8 boycotts, overridden shortlist and will. The pre-arranged-pact version scores only 30% — the plan was overridden, not executed.

hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — HELD 82%
hypotheses.d: HELD. The promised authenticated footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders still has not landed, so the falsifier remains un-run. The week was IRGC-forward — the Guard, not the foreign ministry, confirmed it ran the Oman channel and announced the revenue-sharing terms, and the Guard made the mine-strike claim — but that is DENIED as a raise under the shared-prediction rule: 'the Guard runs the maritime file' is predicted just as strongly by an ordinary reading in which the IRGC is a powerful institution under a functioning Supreme Leader, which is a much weaker claim than 'the IRGC rules Iran'. The 82% cap stands for exactly the reason it was set.

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Held at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: Nobody's hurrying on Hormuz — 60% → 65% (RAISED)
hypotheses.d: Its first fact that BEATS a rival instead of merely fitting itself. On 30 Aug the US struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak after observing Guard personnel preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the strait — two days after CENTCOM declared the lanes fully cleared, and while Muscat negotiates a minesweeping calendar. The 08-30 audit had installed a genuine rival — a physical clock, minesweeping simply takes time — and ruled this hypothesis must beat it. A physical clock runs down; this one is being rewound, by the exact actor the hypothesis named in advance. Capped at +5 on three counts kept in front: CENTCOM is the interested party and 'observed preparations' is unpublished intelligence used to justify a strike; Al Jazeera published a technical challenge on 31 Aug to whether Iran can even mine by rocket as claimed; and IRGC counter-coercion against a blockade that has redirected 83 vessels, disabled three and boarded two explains the same act without any rent motive. Not pre-event.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — HELD 60%, tell sharpened
hypotheses.d: August continues the signature: 125 PLA aerial ADIZ incursions (the 2026 decline intact) against 152 non-warship PRC vessels in the first 21 days, ~60% coast guard, with the east-of-Taiwan patrols now a declared 'new normal'. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up. NOT moved — this is the same signal that bought +5 on 08-26, and re-marking on the continuation of its own evidence is the double-count the audit named. The important item is against my own test: if Beijing has DECLARED the patrols permanent, their persistence through the Sept 24 visit is close to uninformative. Re-specified now, in advance and stricter — the informative observation on 09-23→09-25 is a boarding, an inspection, or a first-time-area incursion. Mere presence no longer counts as confirmation.

hypotheses.name: Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it holds at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Falsifiers: token export volumes, Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing not actually swinging off the Middle East, or the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appearing. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Note it is DISTINCT from 'The Portfolio State' below, which is about the vehicle rather than the motive.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — HELD 52%
hypotheses.d: Confirming but shared, therefore ambience: Treasury again held back on Chinese financial institutions, with mainstream reporting now naming the mechanism outright — designating them 'could create tensions before Xi's visit'. Bessent's promised weekly cadence hit banks but no Chinese one, and at the G20 he pushed severing Iran financial ties while China dissented. Both the leverage read and the ordinary 'Washington won't detonate its own summit' read predict all of it. The strongest weekly argument AGAINST, logged rather than absorbed: the US struck Iran on three consecutive nights and took Iranian fire onto three Arab host states. Deliberate slow-walking for leverage sits badly with sustained kinetic escalation that raises the cost of the thing being slow-walked — that counterweight is what holds the number at 52.

hypotheses.name: A pre-announcement leak into oil futures — 40% → 34% (biggest mover)
hypotheses.d: Its lead conditional has now gone unfired across three weeks containing the most violently market-moving Iran news since April — the 30 Aug Larak strike, three nights of exchanges, two struck VLCCs, Brent to ~$95 — with not one reported nine-figure pre-announcement episode. The file is confirmed as historical and bounded: DOJ is probing four trades totalling ~$2.6bn, all inside a five-week window that closed in April — Mar 23 (>$500m, ~15 min before Trump's delay post), Apr 7 ($960m before the ceasefire), Apr 17 ($760m, ~20 min before Iran said Hormuz was open), Apr 21 ($430m before the extension). CORRECTION BANKED AGAINST THIS ENTRY: the ledger's earlier '~$2.2bn cluster' for Mar 23 and its '~$7bn' aggregate are both withdrawn as over-wide constructions. The cut is made on the hypothesis's own written terms, not on a preferred reading — a conditional set at 60% has burned three of fourteen weeks in the best environment it will ever get and produced nothing. The cut is only −6 because of one genuinely new structural fact: investigators are running a SEPARATE probe into prediction-market activity on the same developments, and the same foreknowledge reaching two unrelated venues is hard to explain as one market-maker hedging client flow. Split now: deliberate leak 34 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 36 / coincidence 10. Still the only entry whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event.

hypotheses.name: NEW · The Portfolio State — coercion converted into sovereign equity, statute retrofitted
hypotheses.d: Strongest form: the US is converting military and sanctions leverage into permanent state equity in strategic supply chains, with the legal authority written to fit transactions rather than the reverse — Venezuela being the first hydrocarbon use of a template already run in chips and critical minerals. The rail predates the headline, which is the only thing licensing a design read at all: Senate NDAA FY2027 §1051 was marked up in MID-JUNE — ten weeks before the 29 Aug deal — creating a DoD Equity Investment Account, authorising OSC equity to $500m and capping any single position at 40% of the entity; the Venezuela stake is 35%, inside a cap that does not legally exist yet. Add DoD's own $400m/15% stake in MP Materials with 100% offtake (structurally identical to Venezuela's '20% of output at cost'), House Oversight already demanding an accounting of Venezuelan oil revenue on 23 Feb, and CFR's tally of 26 government equity deals worth ~$23.9bn. It opens at only 25% because the boring, incompetence and patronage readings are all strong: think tanks have been publicly naming and counting this pattern since 2025 (a policy, not a plot); the Pentagon's own spokesman flatly DENIES that OSC takes equity while WSJ reports it doing so, which is improvisation not design; and a 100-year concession over 65bn bbl routed to one politically connected operator with no published contract is better explained as spoils allocation. Above all the base rate is enormous — Anglo-Persian 1914, the RFC, GM/Chrysler 2009 — so the design premium must be small. NOT a conspiracy claim and must never be scored as one: it requires no secrecy at all, only anticipation, and the honest gap is that I cannot name the operator who executes the warrants. Key test: does the ENACTED NDAA widen §1051 beyond critical minerals to energy, or raise the cap, by 31 Dec (45%)? Scope enacted unchanged kills the design read.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 25% → 22% (CUT, sixth session running)
hypotheses.d: The week finally produced Russia-Iran material and it is the wrong KIND. Moscow said publicly on 01 Sep that air defence is the main focus of military-technical cooperation with Iran, alongside a reported 500 Verba MANPADS and 2,500 missiles and continued fighter deliveries. That is the resupply leg — already priced at 7/10 under 'means'. It moves nothing: it is announced by TASS, an interested party publishing its own helpfulness and the structural opposite of a covert channel; the opportunism branch predicts arms sales to a client at war identically, so under the standing rule it is ambience; and after six sessions there is still ZERO documentary evidence Moscow has influenced Tehran's negotiating position, which is the actual claim. Arms transfers are not persuasion. Cut rather than held because a decay rule that bites only on its deadline is a cliff, not decay. Clock unchanged: 15% on 30 Sep absent documentary evidence, retire below 10%.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Nothing resolved this week, and one file addition cuts against it: the summit's Iran content is now openly reported as an explicit US ask — Chinese pressure on Tehran to reopen the strait — with Beijing expected to want Taiwan concessions in return. An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: Houthis seize Mocha and close on the Bab el-Mandeb strait
brief.h: Ansar Allah took the Red Sea port city of Mocha and the Hais district on Thursday after government forces withdrew under what an Al Jazeera correspondent described as overwhelming military pressure; General Tareq Saleh, whose National Resistance forces held the western coast, reported dead and wounded and ordered his command to reorganise at an alternative headquarters, while Yemeni military sources said the Houthis were also attacking Dhubab and the Hanish islands and seeking the whole Yemeni Red Sea coastline.
brief.t: Mocha sits under fifty miles north of a strait about twenty kilometres wide that carries something like a tenth of world seaborne trade, and the thing that changed on Thursday is not firepower - the Houthis have had anti-ship missiles for three years - it is geography. Holding the coast means you no longer need a missile to interdict: artillery and observation from the shore are enough to make an underwriter nervous, and the nervousness IS the weapon. Follow the money and the target turns out not to be the world's container fleet at all. Saudi Arabia has spent two years trying to leave this war on terms that leave its client forces standing, and the client force has just lost the ground it was standing on. Which is why the Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdulsalam went out the same day to say navigation is safe and regular - a chokepoint you close pays you once, a chokepoint you can close pays you continuously.
brief.context: The rail predates the headline. The 2022 UN truce froze a front line rather than ending a war, and the western coast has been held since 2018 not by the internationally recognised government but by Tareq Saleh's National Resistance, an Emirati-built force nominally on the government's side that was never fully integrated into it - which is why a withdrawal there produces a reorganisation rather than a counterattack. The desk that decides what happens next is not Riyadh's foreign ministry but the London marine war-risk market, because a second Houthi chokepoint only becomes a world event when protection-and-indemnity cover reprices, and that repricing is triggered by underwriter perception rather than by an attack. The base rate is instructive: through 2024 and 2025 the Houthis fired on shipping for more than a year without ever closing Bab el-Mandeb. What would change the read is a strike on a hull with no Saudi link - Lloyd's List Intelligence reports the industry currently believes the threat is confined to Saudi-linked tonnage, and that belief is the only thing holding transits near their recent level.

angles.effect: gains - a second chokepoint held from land, coercive leverage that costs nothing to maintain and can be exercised without firing
gains - a Red Sea card that raises the price of any settlement over Hormuz, at no cost in Iranian materiel or Iranian casualties
pays - the client force it underwrote on the western coast has lost the coast, removing the exit ramp from a war Riyadh has been trying to leave since 2022

angles.party: Tareq Saleh's National Resistance and the coastal population
angles.effect: pay - dead and wounded, a headquarters relocated, and a front that no longer has a hinterland
pay - the Cape of Good Hope reroute adds roughly ten days to a voyage whether or not a single shot is fired

dec.kill: An attack on a hull with no Saudi link, or a war-risk quotation for Bab el-Mandeb that reprices the whole trade rather than Saudi-linked tonnage. Either ends the reading that the Houthis are holding the strait as a bargaining asset rather than as a blockade. Conversely, weekly transits staying near their recent average through the end of September confirms the seizure bought position, not closure.

consp.claim: That the Yemeni government line on the west coast did not break, it was sold - that Saudi and Emirati backers cut a quiet deal handing the Houthis the coastline in exchange for an end to strikes on Saudi energy facilities, timed to Riyadh's need to get out before the war reaches its own refineries. A louder version alongside it reads the collapse as proof that Gulf client armies are hollow by construction and the entire Saudi position in Yemen is American-financed theatre.
consp.spread: A /pol/ thread reporting the coastline seizure ran to 120 replies, and a gloating thread framed around Saudi forces folding days after their backers floated an Assad-style ending for the Houthis reached 144; the board's Persia-Israel general, now on edition 2,093, carried the story all day.
consp.read: This maps onto the sold-out-by-your-patron frame applied to Kabul in 2021 and to Syrian army units in 2024, and it has a real kernel: Riyadh has openly sought an exit since the 2022 truce and the Houthis did strike Saudi energy facilities this week, so a trade of coast for calm is a coherent thing for a principal to want. What the theory cannot survive is the sequencing - Saudi aircraft flew roughly forty strikes on Houthi positions the day before the city fell, which is not how a handover looks. Prefer the boring read: an Emirati-built militia never integrated into the national army withdrew when its patrons would not reinforce it.

brief.head: Oil hits $105 as Treasury yields reach a three-year high
brief.h: Brent traded at $105 a barrel for the first time since May and WTI touched $100 before easing to about $99, both up more than four per cent on the day, while the ten-year Treasury yield rose nine basis points to about 4.93 per cent - its highest since October 2023 - the thirty-year pushed through 5.30 per cent, the S&P 500 fell half a per cent for a fourth straight session, and August producer prices came in at 0.4 per cent on the month and 5.4 per cent on the year against 5.3 expected, with diesel up 24.1 per cent accounting for over a third of the increase in final-demand goods.
brief.t: This is the configuration the desk has been waiting for and it is the least cinematic one: an energy shock arriving through the middle of the price index rather than at the pump. Diesel is the tell, because diesel is not a consumer good, it is the cost of moving every other good - the national average hit a record $5.98 a gallon - so a 24 per cent monthly jump propagates into food, freight and construction on a one-to-two-quarter lag, which is exactly the window in which the Federal Reserve has to decide. Futures now put a hike at next Wednesday's meeting at about seventy per cent, up from forty-nine a week ago. And note who is NOT being consoled: Treasury announced a buyback of up to six billion dollars of long-dated debt, triple the usual size, and yields rose anyway, because the market had priced seven to ten. Mike O'Rourke of JonesTrading called it shooting a BB gun at an elephant.
brief.context: The rail here is a debt calendar, not a war. Treasury's problem is that a buyback swaps which bond you hold without changing how many bonds exist - the deficit runs near 1.8 trillion dollars a year and every dollar of it returns as supply - so the operators to watch are the primary dealers and the SOMA desk, not the podium. The question underneath is whether the Fed tightens INTO a supply shock, historically the configuration that breaks levered positions somewhere else first. The base rate is the honest constraint on all of it: central banks have never reversed an energy-driven price rise, only the demand it feeds into, which is why a hike next week would be aimed at expectations rather than at barrels. S&P Global's Jim Burkhard says the market is adjusting to a new normal defined by unresolved conflict, and the firm no longer assumes Middle East output returns to pre-war levels by the end of 2027. What would change the read is core PPI, which rose 0.2 per cent against 0.3 expected - the shock has not yet become general.

angles.effect: gains a headline - a buyback tripled in size reads as decisive action and cost nothing politically to announce
pay - the operation was smaller than priced, so the announcement itself moved yields against them
gain - the crack spread on diesel is where the money in this shock actually is, not in crude
pay - diesel is an input cost with no substitute on a one-year horizon

angles.party: Anyone rolling debt this quarter, sovereign or corporate
angles.effect: pays - the term premium is the transmission channel and it is repricing globally, with European government yields at fifteen-year highs

dec.kill: Core PPI or core CPI accelerating above 0.3 per cent on the month would move this from an energy shock to a general inflation, and make the Fed's decision about wages rather than barrels. In the other direction, a buyback clearing at seven billion or more with yields falling alongside it would show Treasury can still set the long end - so far it cannot.

consp.claim: That the Strategic Petroleum Reserve is already empty and the record diesel print is the market discovering it. Running alongside: that the Treasury Secretary is deliberately letting the long end go to force the Federal Reserve's hand, and a harder version claiming the buyback was never meant to work and exists to supply an alibi for when thirty-year yields go through six per cent.
consp.spread: A /pol/ thread asking whether the spike means the reserves are about to run out, a diesel-record happening thread cross-posted to /biz/ where it drew 86 replies, an oil-to-$150 thread at 47 built on a viral post from a television market host, and a /biz/ thread asking whether this Treasury Secretary will go down as the most destructive of all time.
consp.read: The hidden-empty-vault frame, and the checkable kernel is real but smaller and more interesting than the claim: SPR levels are published, the reserve was never refilled to pre-2022 levels, and crucially it holds crude, not distillate - a crude reserve cannot fix a refined-products shortage. Rystad's Claudio Galimberti made exactly that point on the record today, calling the products crisis more dangerous than the crude move. The Treasury half is downstream of a genuine embarrassment rather than evidence of intent: the buyback was tripled and yields rose anyway, which is what happens when a market is bigger than an operation.

brief.head: ECB hikes into an energy shock its forecasts cannot see
brief.h: The European Central Bank raised its deposit rate a quarter point to 2.5 per cent, the main refinancing rate to 2.65 and the marginal lending facility to 2.9 - its second hike in three months - after euro-area inflation rose to 3.3 per cent in August on energy up 14.3 per cent year on year, while core fell to 2.4 and services to 3.0, and said the conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflationary pressure and that inflation will remain well above target for an extended period.
brief.t: Read the two halves of that print against each other, because they point in opposite directions. Energy at 14.3 per cent is an import bill - a transfer of European income to whoever sells the barrel. Core at 2.4 and services falling to 3.0 say the shock has not become a wage-price spiral. A central bank tightening against the first of those is not fighting inflation, it is demonstrating that it will not let expectations drift; the rate is aimed at the forecast, not at the gas. The detail that matters most is buried in the staff projections: their data cut-off falls roughly two weeks before the meeting, so neither Brent's move to $105 nor the surge in European government bond yields to fifteen-year highs is in the numbers the Governing Council just voted on. They raised the 2027 and 2028 forecasts anyway - to 2.5 and 2.1 per cent.
brief.context: The epoch rail is the 2022 gas rupture, which Europe solved by replacing Russian pipeline gas with seaborne LNG and thereby converting a political dependency into a price dependency: Europe now buys energy at whatever the world charges, which makes every Middle East chokepoint a European domestic policy problem. The desk that decides is not Frankfurt but the national treasuries, because a fifteen-year high in government yields lands on countries whose defence budgets are rising in the same quarter as their energy import bill. The base rate is the one the ECB knows and cannot say out loud: no central bank has offset an energy supply shock with rates, only the demand behind it - so the mechanism by which this hike lowers headline inflation runs through European demand and therefore through European growth. What would change the read is core: if it turns up from 2.4 toward 3, the shock has gone general and the hike was early rather than performative.

angles.effect: gains - acting into a shock is how a central bank buys the right to be believed later, and it costs nothing this quarter

angles.party: Euro-area savers and the currency's external value
angles.effect: gain modestly - the dollar still strengthened on the day, but a wider policy gap would have been worse
pay - a higher policy rate lands on top of government yields already at fifteen-year highs
pays twice - the input cost and the cost of money at once; Volkswagen earmarked 16 billion euros for job cuts and plant closures the same day
gain - the transfer is real and it is denominated in euros leaving the continent

dec.kill: Core inflation turning up from 2.4 per cent, or negotiated wage growth accelerating, would vindicate the hike as pre-emption. If core keeps falling while headline stays high, the ECB has tightened into an income transfer it cannot influence - and the next projection round, built on data that actually includes $105 Brent, will have to say so.

consp.claim: That Europe is being deliberately deindustrialised - that the energy shock is not a side effect of a Middle East war but the mechanism, with American LNG and American-aligned finance the beneficiaries, and that European central banks are raising rates to accelerate rather than cushion it. The board version is blunter: the United States can secure barrels wherever it likes while Europeans are priced back to pre-industrial transport.
consp.spread: A /pol/ thread built around Brent being out of control drew 152 replies making exactly this argument, and the German and British generals on the same board carried the energy-price framing through the day.
consp.read: The managed-decline frame, whose kernel is a real structural fact rather than a plan: Europe swapped pipeline dependency for seaborne LNG in 2022, which genuinely does transfer pricing power to exporters and genuinely does hit energy-intensive manufacturing hardest - Volkswagen's 16 billion euro restructuring the same day is the visible cost. What the theory adds is intent, and intent is the part with no rail behind it; the identical outcome follows from a continent that had no fast alternative and made the only substitution available. Watch industrial electricity prices and German industrial output rather than the rhetoric.

brief.head: Trump offers Americans $5,000 if Republicans hold Congress
brief.h: At the Republican National Committee's first-ever midterm convention in Dallas, President Trump promised a $5,000 dividend to every American citizen conditional on Republicans holding both the House and the Senate in November - "If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000" - and suggested tariff revenue would partly fund it; paid to roughly 245 million adult citizens the cost would exceed one trillion dollars, and it would require an act of Congress that does not exist.
brief.t: Price the promise the way a desk would, by asking what it costs the person making it. A conditional transfer that requires legislation nobody has drafted, in a Congress that must first exist, funded by a revenue stream that has collected just under 500 billion dollars since the start of last year and has already refunded more than 100 billion of it after the Supreme Court struck down much of the tariff schedule - that is not a fiscal proposal, it is a campaign instrument with a price tag attached to make it feel real. The tell is the conditionality itself: a policy you intend to enact is not made contingent on an election result, because the election result is what lets you enact it. The second tell is the ask - "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot, just one more time" - a president who cannot be on the ballot trying to convert personal turnout into congressional turnout, the hardest transfer in American politics.
brief.context: There is a rail here and it is a short one: this is the third iteration of the same instrument. A DOGE-savings dividend was floated, then a $2,000 tariff dividend promised for mid-2026, and neither arrived - which is the base rate that should govern how anyone prices the third. The desk that decides is the House Ways and Means Committee and the Senate parliamentarian, not the podium: a direct payment this size is either an appropriation or a refundable credit, both of which need a bill and a score, and the CBO score would land in an environment where thirty-year yields have just pushed through 5.30 per cent. That collision happened on the same day - a trillion-dollar spending promise announced into a bond market that spent the session telling the Treasury it does not want more duration. Watch whether the promise survives contact with the Treasury Secretary, who has previously said plainly that Congress would have to authorise these payments.

angles.effect: gain - a concrete number attached to a vote, the most efficient turnout instrument available, and it costs nothing until after the election
gains - a way to put himself on a ballot he is not on
pays - a trillion-dollar promise priced into a long end already at three-year-high yields, on a day its own buyback failed to move them
pay - this is the third version of the same dividend and the first two never arrived
pays - the tariff revenue named as the source has been partly refunded by court order, so the offset does not exist

dec.kill: Introduced legislation with a sponsor, a number and a CBO score before November. If no bill text exists by election day, this was a turnout instrument and the ledger should score it as one. The reverse test is equally clean: the Treasury Secretary endorsing a specific funding mechanism on the record would move this from framing toward a real proposal.

consp.claim: That the $5,000 promise is a straightforward vote purchase that will never be paid, the proof being that the DOGE savings dividend and the $2,000 tariff checks were both promised and never arrived - and, in the market-facing version, that the announcement is a trial balloon for monetising 1.35 trillion dollars of new issuance, floated deliberately to see what the ten and thirty-year do before anyone commits.
consp.spread: Very loud. The lead /pol/ thread ran to 307 replies, a thread doing the arithmetic on printing 1.35 trillion reached 139, a thread stacking DOGE plus tariff plus dividend into a claimed $12,000 per citizen drew 66, and it crossed to /biz/ where a thread framing it as a 1.5 trillion stimulus and asking what it does to the US10Y and US30Y ran to 55 alongside a viral finance-account post.
consp.read: The never-arriving half is not a theory, it is a track record - two prior dividends announced, neither paid - and it is the correct base rate to price this one at. The monetisation half is the interesting one and it is checkable: a genuine trial balloon would produce a Treasury follow-up within days, either walking the funding claim back or naming a mechanism. Silence would suggest the promise was aimed at voters and never at the bond market at all.

brief.head: Algeria cuts ties with the UAE and gives its envoy 48 hours
brief.h: Algeria's foreign ministry severed diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates on Thursday, saying it had exhausted all means of preserving bilateral relations and citing provocative or hostile Emirati actions; the Emirati ambassador was summoned and given 48 hours to comply, and there was no immediate response from Abu Dhabi.
brief.t: A rupture this total between two states with no shared border and little trade is not about the bilateral relationship - it is about the three files where they already fight through other people. Western Sahara, where the UAE recognises Moroccan sovereignty and runs a consulate in the territory while Algeria hosts and arms the Polisario Front. The Abraham Accords, which Algiers has treated as a betrayal since 2020. And the Sahel, where Emirati money and security relationships have expanded into exactly the junta-run states that broke with Algeria after their coups. Follow the money and the Sahel is the live one: Algeria's leverage south of its border used to be geography and gas, and it is being displaced by a Gulf state that arrives with capital, drones and no colonial history. President Tebboune said the quiet part in July - wherever they set foot, blood flows - and called the UAE a statelet.
brief.context: The rail is 1975 and it never closed: the Western Sahara conflict has structured North African alignment for fifty years, and every outside power that picks Morocco is automatically picking against Algiers. What is new is the vector. The UAE has spent a decade converting oil revenue into ports, drone transfers and security partnerships across the Red Sea littoral and the Sahel, and Algeria - a hydrocarbon state with an ageing export base and a shrinking sphere - is watching a rival buy influence it used to inherit. The desk that decides here is Sonatrach and the gas contracts, not the foreign ministry, because Algeria's real instruments are pipelines into Spain and Italy and a large arms relationship with Russia; a diplomatic rupture with a Gulf state costs it almost nothing, which is exactly why it is affordable as a signal. Base rate on ruptures of this class - Morocco-Algeria in 2021, Morocco-Iran in 2018 - they last years and change little on the ground. What would change the read is Emirati action in the Sahel that Algeria treats as a security matter rather than a diplomatic one.

angles.effect: gains - a nationalist gesture with almost no economic cost, delivered to a domestic audience amid a shrinking regional position
gains - its principal Gulf backer is now formally the adversary of its principal rival, hardening a coalition Rabat has built since 2020
largely unaffected - the relationships being fought over are with Bamako, Ouagadougou and Niamey, none of which were consulted
pays - a louder patron is not a stronger one, and the channel that might have moderated Emirati support for Rabat is now closed

angles.party: Algerian citizens and workers in the Gulf
angles.effect: pay - consular services are the first casualty of a severance and there is no replacement channel

dec.kill: Emirati or Algerian action in the Sahel that goes beyond statements - an arms transfer, a base agreement or a security pact with one of the junta states naming the other. Absent that, this is a signal and should be scored as one. Gulf mediation restoring the mission within six months would confirm the low-cost reading.

watch: Bab el-Mandeb transit counts for the weeks to 13 and 20 September. Lloyd's List Intelligence tracked 302 passings in the week to 23 August and an average of 273 a week against a pre-blockade 319, on an explicit industry assumption that the Houthi threat is confined to Saudi-linked tonnage. That assumption is the only thing holding the number up, and Mocha is the test of it.

A war-risk quotation for Bab el-Mandeb that stops distinguishing Saudi-linked hulls from the general trade. The Houthis do not need to fire to close the strait; they need underwriters to believe they might. This is the observable that converts a land advance into a world event.

Core CPI on the month, then the FOMC on 16 September. Core PPI printed 0.2 against 0.3 expected - the one number still saying this is an energy shock rather than a general inflation. lesson: Today's lesson is about proxies, and it explains why this board refused to raise its Iran forecast on a day when Iranian-aligned forces set Saudi oil sites on fire. When a state fights through someone else's army, it is buying a specific product: deniability. Idean Salehyan's work on the delegation of war to non-state groups sets out the trade - the sponsor gets cheapness and a plausible shrug, and pays for it with a principal-agent problem, because the proxy has its own war aims and can drag the sponsor somewhere it did not choose to go. Thomas Schelling's companion idea is that the ambiguity is not a bug: an attack nobody can cleanly attribute is a threat that is hard to answer without escalating first, which is why the wrapper is worth paying for. The base rate is where this stops being theory. On 14 September 2019, drones and cruise missiles knocked 5.7 million barrels a day - half of Saudi output - out of Abqaiq and Khurais; the Houthis claimed it, Washington publicly blamed Iran, UN monitors later found the Houthis could not have done it, and the American response was a troop deployment and sanctions, not a strike on Iran. So here is the discipline the lesson yields, and it is testable: attribution is not a trigger, ownership is. Watch whether anything hits an ASSET the United States must answer for - a US-flagged hull, an American casualty - because that, not the size of the fire in Jazan, is the variable that has historically moved American decisions.

quiz.q: Iranian-aligned forces set fire to Saudi oil facilities, and this board did NOT raise its forecast of a renewed US or Israeli strike campaign on Iran. What is the stated reason?
options: Because the attack was too small to matter to oil markets
Because in 2019 a far larger attack on Saudi oil - Abqaiq, half the kingdom's output - produced no American strike on Iran
Because the Houthis are not connected to Iran in any way
Because the US has publicly ruled out further strikes on Iran
quiz.why: The base rate is the discipline. Abqaiq removed 5.7 million barrels a day, was blamed on Iran by Washington, and produced a troop deployment and sanctions - not a strike. Damage to Saudi assets has historically not been the trigger; damage to American ones has, which is why this board's CRITICAL gate is a struck US-flagged hull or an American death rather than a burning refinery.

quiz.q: The brief says the Jazan complex is the asset that converts a Yemeni grievance into a global price. Why Jazan specifically rather than the size of any fire?
options: Because Jazan is where most Saudi crude is loaded for export
Because it is a 400,000 b/d refinery, about a tenth of Aramco's net refining capacity, and the world is short conversion capacity rather than crude
Because it is the closest facility to Iran
Because Jazan produces most of Saudi Arabia's electricity
quiz.why: A barrel of crude is not a usable product. The binding constraint in this cycle is the capacity to turn crude into diesel, so hitting a refinery bites harder per unit of damage than hitting a wellhead. Crude exports load at Ras Tanura and Yanbu, hundreds of miles from anything struck on Tuesday - which is why the brief's kill criterion is loadings, not fires.

quiz.q: Russia paused strikes on Kyiv for exactly the 72 hours that US envoys were in the region, then fired 166 drones. What does the brief say that timing reveals?
options: That Russia is running out of missiles and needed to reload
That Moscow can switch the air campaign on and off at will, which indicates confidence rather than exhaustion
That the pause was imposed on Russia by the United States
That Ukraine's air defences were down during the visit
quiz.why: A truce whose duration matches an itinerary to the hour is a scheduling accommodation, not a de-escalation - and the precision is itself the information. Fortna's finding is that ceasefires without monitors, guarantors or a demilitarised separation fail at high rates, and this arrangement had none of the three, which is why the 30-day ceasefire forecast was cut rather than raised.

quiz.q: The brief argues that stablecoins and the Fed's bill programme cannot fix Britain's 5.89 per cent thirty-year yield. What is the mechanism?
options: Because those programmes create demand for SHORT paper - bills - so the bid concentrates at the front of the curve and the long end is left to private buyers
Because the Bank of England is prohibited from buying gilts
Because stablecoins are illegal in the United Kingdom
Because thirty-year debt is not sold at auction
quiz.why: Tokenised dollar claims have to be backed by something short and liquid, which means Treasury bills. That manufactures a bid at the front end and does nothing for thirty-year duration, which is left to pension funds, insurers and price-sensitive foreigners who charge for inflation risk. Hence the brief's line that the long end is the leg no monetary innovation repairs.

quiz.q: CRITICAL THINKING. A widely circulated report puts transshipment - Chinese goods relabelled through third countries - at up to $303bn. Which observable best tests that CLAIM?
options: Whether the total Chinese trade surplus keeps rising
Whether more governments publicly endorse the report
Whether the rerouting rate holds up when customs data are matched WITHIN individual firms rather than at the product level
Whether Vietnam's exports to the US grew faster than its exports elsewhere
quiz.why: The size of the number depends almost entirely on how coarsely you match the data. Academic work found about 16.5 per cent of US-bound Vietnamese exports looked rerouted at the national product level, 6.5 per cent within provinces, and 1.7 per cent within individual firms - meaning aggregation was mistaking one company's genuine production for another's rerouting. The claim is checkable, and the check is firm-level matching.

sections.t: US diesel set an all-time record this week at $5.820 a gallon, and the crack spread — the refiner's fee for turning crude into something an engine can burn — printed an all-time $108 a barrel while Brent sat at an unremarkable $96. In the same week US missiles reportedly struck a tanker at Iran's Kharg Island anchorage, and Ukrainian drones held Russian refinery runs at 3.6m barrels a day, the lowest since May 2002.

Crude — the thing everyone photographs and embargoes — is behaving; refined product is not. A $108 crack means the market will pay more to convert a barrel than the barrel is worth: a fact about cokers and hydrotreaters, not about oil. Name the mechanism — the conversion bottleneck. The binding constraint is never the abundant input but the narrow step in the middle, which cannot be built on the timescale of a war or an election.

sections.h: Deep history I — Rockefeller never wanted the oil
sections.t: John D. Rockefeller owned almost no wells. He owned the refineries of Cleveland, and what he did with them in 1871 is the founding text of chokepoint economics. Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad chartered the South Improvement Company, and Rockefeller's terms inside it were breathtaking: the Erie, New York Central and Pennsylvania would pay the SIC a rebate of $1.06 on every barrel it shipped — and a drawback of $1.06 on every barrel shipped by refiners outside the club. He was paid when his rivals did business. The charter was repealed that April before a single transaction cleared, and Ida Tarbell's exposé later finished the job — but the insight outlived the scandal: crude is worthless until someone converts and moves it, and whoever owns the narrow step prices the wide one.

sections.h: Deep history II — the war decided at the still
sections.t: The largest test of this proposition was the Allied air war, fought inside the alliance before it was fought over Germany. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command believed in punishment: burn the cities, break the will. Carl Spaatz and Arthur Tedder pushed what Harris dismissed as panacea targets — oil. Germany had almost no crude. It had Bergius hydrogenation, synthetic fuel pressed from coal at Leuna, Pölitz and Brüx, plants too enormous to hide. The oil plan began in May 1944. Leuna alone absorbed 22 raids, 6,552 bomber sorties and 18,328 tons of bombs across a year, behind Europe's heaviest flak concentration. It worked anyway. German synthetic output fell from a peak of 316,000 tons a month to 107,000 in June 1944 and 17,000 by September. Aviation gasoline — the specific fraction, not oil in general — went from 175,000 tons in April to 5,000 in September: 97% gone in five months. From May 1944 Germany consumed more than it produced every month, and the stockpile was gone in six.

sections.h: Deep history II — the fuel, not the factories
sections.t: The detail that makes it unforgettable: over the same period Albert Speer drove German tank and aircraft PRODUCTION to its wartime peak. The Reich ended 1944 with more airframes than it could fly and more panzers than it could move — the factories were fine and the fuel was not. The US Strategic Bombing Survey — written by people with every reason to praise bombing in general — judged the oil and transport campaigns decisive and the city campaign not. Japan lost the same way: the July 1941 freeze is remembered as an oil embargo, but the fatal shortage was 100-octane aviation gasoline, a conversion capability Japan could not build.

sections.h: Deep history III — how the West stopped building stills
sections.t: Now the slow part. The last greenfield major refinery built in the United States was Marathon's Garyville, Louisiana: built 1973-76, online 1977, still running at 596,000 barrels a day. Fifty years, no new plants — and the base is now shrinking: about 132 operable refineries in January 2025 against more than 300 in 1981, with roughly 1.235m b/d of distillation capacity removed in seven recent closures and conversions, over 6.5% of the total. All of it while shale made America the largest crude producer in history at 13.86m b/d. The country built the well and stopped building the still. The capacity emigrated rather than vanished — Jamnagar runs 1.24m b/d, Dangote opened at 650,000 and plans 1.4m, China kept building — so the toll moved east and south, to jurisdictions happy to buy discounted sanctioned crude and sell the product back to the people imposing the sanctions.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: In all three cases the scarce thing is the transformation, and transformation capacity is inelastic over any politically relevant horizon: a new crude supplier takes a fortnight, a new hydrocracker takes five years and a billion dollars. Ukraine is now running the 1944 oil plan at a ten-thousandth of the cost, a drone flying 1,550km to Omsk doing what 6,552 B-17 sorties did to Leuna — Pape's denial thesis tested live. It breaks against me here: Germany had no crude and no neutral supplier, Russia has both, and a 24-year low in refining has not stopped Pokrovsk.

sections.h: The adjudication — Yergin and Blas vs Chris Miller
sections.t: THE ADJUDICATION — YERGIN AND BLAS versus CHRIS MILLER Yergin and Blas hold that energy chokepoints self-heal — inventories, bypass and rerouting absorb shocks forecast to be fatal — and they have been right about the barrel, Brent at $96 in a war that curtailed over 11m b/d. Chris Miller's Chip War argues the opposite for inputs that are not fungible: no reserve of fabs, no bypass for EUV, a decade to rebuild. The evidence splits them by step. Yergin and Blas won the crude argument; the crack is the market announcing the win does not survive one step downstream, because there is no strategic reserve of cokers — the US holds hundreds of millions of barrels of crude in the SPR and about a million barrels of distillate in the Northeast reserve, having stockpiled the input it cannot burn. Miller's case is still weaker in oil than in silicon: diesel is shippable in a way a fab's output is not, so refining heals in 12-24 months rather than 12-24 days.

OECD gasoline demand is in structural decline as EVs scale; diesel and jet demand are not, because trucks, ships, aircraft, mining and data-centre backup have no substitute. But a refinery makes every cut at once, so the economics that close Western refineries — falling gasoline — destroy the distillate capacity nobody meant to lose. A trap, not a cycle; confidence high. The bolder call, near 60%: by the mid-2030s the US is at once the world's largest crude exporter and a chronic net importer of middle distillates, and that buys a strategic PRODUCT reserve — legislated storage of diesel and jet, enacted after a winter shortage rather than before one. What keeps this honest is GEO-026: does the US diesel crack settle below $45 before 15 December 2026? It sits at 35%, so the house is 65% on regime rather than outage — and if the crack mean-reverts on the 2022 schedule, this is an elegant story about a spike, published as a miss.
